title: HTTP and REST API design
blurb: Methods, status codes, idempotency, headers, caching, versioning. The highest-value non-code topic on the whole path — it comes up in frontend, backend and fullstack interviews alike.

questions.q: Which HTTP methods are defined as idempotent?
choices: GET and HEAD only, since they are the only methods that never change state
POST and PATCH, because the server can detect and skip a repeated request
GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE: repeating one leaves the same end state
Every method at all, provided the client resends a byte-identical request body
questions.why: Idempotent means N identical requests have the same effect on the server as one. DELETE twice leaves it deleted (the second may return 404, which is fine). GET and HEAD are safe as well as idempotent; PUT and DELETE change state but idempotently. POST is not, which is why double-submits create duplicate orders.
questions.asked: Extremely common, because it explains retries, double-submits and payment bugs.

questions.q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
choices: PUT only ever creates resources; PATCH only ever updates existing ones
PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH applies a partial change to it
PATCH is a newer alias for PUT, and servers must treat them identically
PUT is for JSON bodies; PATCH is for form-encoded bodies from HTML forms
questions.why: A PUT that omits a field should clear it, because you sent the full representation. PATCH sends only what changes, which is why "field absent" vs "field set to null" matters so much in a PATCH payload. PUT can also create a resource at a URI the client chooses.
questions.asked: A phone-screen staple; the absent-vs-null follow-up shows whether you have built a PATCH endpoint.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 401 response from a 403?
choices: 401 is for an expired token; 403 is for a request with no token at all
401 means not authenticated; 403 means authenticated but not allowed
401 is for API clients; 403 is the same error when shown to a browser
403 means the resource does not exist; 401 means it exists but is locked
questions.why: 401 (despite its name, "Unauthorized") means "who are you?" and should carry a WWW-Authenticate header; an expired token is a 401 too. 403 means logging in again will not help. Some APIs deliberately return 404 instead of 403 to avoid revealing that a resource exists.
questions.asked: Asked constantly, and easy to get right, so getting it wrong stands out.

questions.q: A request body fails validation. Which status should the API return?
choices: 500, because the server could not complete the request as sent
404, because no resource matching the submitted data exists yet
400, or 422 if you separate malformed syntax from invalid content
200 with an error field, so every client parses replies the same way
questions.why: 4xx says the client must change the request; 500 says the server failed and invites a retry. 422 is the finer-grained "valid JSON, invalid content". Returning 200 with `{ error }` breaks every generic HTTP client, retry policy and monitoring dashboard.
questions.asked: Checks you know status codes are a contract with clients and monitoring, not decoration.

questions.q: What does 409 Conflict mean in practice?
choices: The server is overloaded and rejects any new writes until its load drops
The client sent two headers whose values contradict one another
Two requests for the same resource reached the server at exactly the same moment
It clashes with current state, such as a duplicate email or a stale version
questions.why: Typical uses: registering an email that already exists, or an optimistic-concurrency failure where the resource changed since the client read it. Overload is 503 (or 429 per client), and two simultaneous requests are only a conflict if one invalidates the other.
questions.asked: Leads straight into how you detect a stale write, which is the interesting part.

questions.q: How should REST resource URLs be named?
choices: Verbs that describe the action, such as /getUserOrders?userId=42
Plural nouns with ids and shallow nesting, such as /users/42/orders
One /api endpoint that takes a command name in the request body
Whatever matches the controller's method names, so code and URL agree
questions.why: The HTTP method is the verb and the URL is the noun. Nest one level at most: `/users/42/orders/7/items/3` is worse than `/order-items/3`. A single command endpoint is RPC, which is a legitimate style but not REST.
questions.asked: A quick check that you have read and designed more than one API.

questions.q: What does a 201 Created response usually include?
choices: An empty body, since the client already has the data it just sent
The full collection, so that the client can refresh its whole list in one go
A redirect to the list page, so a browser refresh cannot resubmit
A Location header for the new resource, and often its representation
questions.why: Returning the created object gives the client the server-assigned id and timestamps without another round trip; 204 is right when there is genuinely nothing to return. Redirect-after-POST is a pattern for HTML form pages (303), not for JSON APIs.
questions.asked: Checks you think about what the client needs next, not just what the server did.

questions.q: How does offset pagination (`?page=3&limit=20`) break on a busy dataset?
choices: It cannot be combined with ORDER BY, so pages arrive in random order
Databases cap OFFSET at 1,000 rows, so deep pages return an error
Inserts and deletes between requests make rows skip or repeat across pages
It needs a total row count, which the database must recompute for every page
questions.why: If a row is inserted before page 3 while the user is on page 2, every later row shifts by one and one is shown twice. Deep offsets are also slow, because the database still walks and discards every row before the offset. Keyset pagination fixes both.
questions.asked: A great question: it needs both API design and database awareness.

questions.q: What is an ETag for?
choices: A checksum the client verifies to detect corruption of the body in transit
A version fingerprint for conditional requests: 304 on reads, 412 on stale writes
An id the server assigns each client so it can track them across requests
A label naming the API release that served the response, for debugging
questions.why: The client sends `If-None-Match` on GET and gets a bodyless 304 if nothing changed. On PUT, `If-Match` lets the server reject a write based on a stale read with 412, which is how HTTP prevents lost updates. Integrity in transit is TLS's job.
questions.asked: Few candidates know the write-side use; naming If-Match is a strong signal.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Cache-Control: no-store` and `no-cache`?
choices: no-cache forbids keeping a copy; no-store keeps one but revalidates it first
They are synonyms; no-cache is simply the HTTP/1.0 spelling of no-store
no-store applies only to shared proxies; no-cache applies only to browsers
no-store forbids keeping a copy; no-cache keeps one but revalidates it first
questions.why: The naming is genuinely backwards, which is why the swapped option is tempting. `no-store` is what you want for sensitive responses. `no-cache` is "check with me first", usually paired with an ETag so the check is cheap. The HTTP/1.0 relic is `Pragma: no-cache`.
questions.asked: A precise question that separates people who have configured caching from those who have read about it.

questions.q: How do you evolve a public API without breaking existing clients?
choices: Bump the version on every release so clients always know what changed
Add fields rather than change them; version only for breaking changes
Never change a published API; build a new one beside it per feature
Add a query parameter per change so clients opt in one at a time
questions.why: Additive changes are compatible as long as clients ignore unknown fields. Breaking changes need a new version and a migration path: run both and give consumers a deprecation window. Versioning every release forces needless migrations.
questions.asked: Checks you have maintained an API that someone else depended on.

questions.q: What should an API error response body contain?
choices: The exception message and stack trace, so client developers can debug it
A plain string message, since the status code already carries the meaning
A consistent shape: a stable code, a human message and field-level details
Nothing at all, because well-behaved clients should branch on the status code alone
questions.why: Clients need to branch on something stable, not on English prose, and forms need to know which field failed. RFC 9457 Problem Details (formerly RFC 7807: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`) is a ready-made shape that ASP.NET Core emits by default. Stack traces belong in logs.
questions.asked: Very common for backend roles. Never leak a stack trace to a client.

questions.q: What does a 429 status mean, and what should accompany it?
choices: Request Timeout, sent with a Keep-Alive header to extend it
Payload Too Large, sent with a Content-Length header to cap it
Too Many Requests, ideally sent with a Retry-After header
Service Unavailable, sent with a Location header to redirect
questions.why: Retry-After tells the client exactly how long to back off, which turns a guess into a contract. Timeout is 408, payload too large 413 and unavailable 503. A well-behaved client honours Retry-After rather than retrying in a tight loop.
questions.asked: Checks you can name the header that makes rate limiting cooperative.

questions.q: Why is a GET endpoint with side effects a problem?
choices: GET requests cannot carry a body, so the change has no data to work with
GET responses are slower, because browsers revalidate them every time
It only breaks naming conventions; clients and proxies treat it exactly the same
Crawlers, prefetchers and caches may issue or replay GETs you never expect
questions.why: GET is defined as safe, so browsers prefetch links, crawlers follow them and retries repeat them. The classic disaster is a `/delete?id=5` link that a crawler walks. Data for a GET travels in the URL, so the lack of a body is not the problem.
questions.asked: The crawler-deleted-everything story is a favourite; it tests whether "safe" means anything to you.

questions.q: What difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 matters to a web developer?
choices: HTTP/2 lets the server skip status codes, as each stream signals success
HTTP/2 drops request headers and moves the metadata into the body
HTTP/2 keeps one request per connection but opens far more of them
HTTP/2 multiplexes requests over one connection, so bundling matters less
questions.why: Under HTTP/1.1 browsers opened about six connections per host and each carried one request at a time, so concatenating files and sharding domains paid off. With multiplexing, many small cacheable files can beat one big bundle. HTTP/2 also compresses headers, making cookies cheaper.
questions.asked: Checks your build and hosting habits are current rather than inherited from 2012.

questions.q: The browser sends this preflight before a cross-origin PUT. What must your server return for the PUT to go ahead?
questions.code:
OPTIONS /api/orders/7 HTTP/1.1
Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization
choices: A 204 with an Allow: PUT header, which browsers read to decide on CORS
A 401 when unauthenticated, as the preflight carries the Authorization header
A 2xx with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods and -Headers covering it
A 200 with the resource body, which the browser reuses for the real PUT
questions.why: The browser checks the Access-Control-Allow-* headers on an ok response against the method and headers it asked about, then sends the PUT. A preflight never carries credentials, so auth middleware that rejects OPTIONS with 401 is a classic cause of mystery CORS failures. `Allow` is unrelated to CORS.
questions.asked: Guaranteed if the role touches a browser and an API on different origins; the 401-on-OPTIONS bug is the follow-up.

questions.q: Where does authentication information belong in an HTTP request?
choices: A query parameter, so the token survives redirects and is easy to test
The request body, so that it is encrypted along with the payload
The Authorization header, or a cookie for browser sessions, never the URL
A custom X-Token header, since Authorization is reserved for HTTP Basic auth
questions.why: URLs end up in browser history, server and proxy logs, and Referer headers, so a token in a query string leaks to everything in the path. Under TLS the headers are encrypted exactly like the body. Authorization carries any scheme, Bearer included.
questions.asked: Checks you know where URLs leak to, which is the whole reason for the rule.

questions.q: What does "REST is stateless" actually mean?
choices: The server stores no data at all, so all application state lives in the client
Each request carries what the server needs; no session lives in memory
Responses cannot be cached, since each depends on the request state
Clients cannot use cookies, since a cookie is state between requests
questions.why: The database is state; a per-connection, in-memory conversation is what REST forbids. A session id in a cookie is fine if the session lives in a shared store. Statelessness is what lets any instance behind a load balancer serve any request.
questions.asked: A conceptual question with a very practical consequence: horizontal scaling.

questions.q: Where do filtering, sorting and search go in a REST API for a collection?
choices: A separate endpoint per filter, such as /orders/open and /orders/by-date
Request headers such as X-Filter-Status, so the URLs stay short and clean
Path segments in a fixed order, such as /orders/status/open/sort/created
Query parameters on the collection: /orders?status=open&sort=-created
questions.why: One resource, many views of it, and the URL stays bookmarkable and cacheable. Headers are invisible in links and are not part of the cache key without `Vary`. Allow-list sortable fields: user input straight into ORDER BY is an injection risk and a surprise table scan.
questions.asked: Checks you design URLs for caching and sharing, not only for your router.

questions.q: What is an idempotency key?
choices: A hash of the request body, which the server then uses as its response cache key
A client-generated id sent with a POST so the server can recognise a retry
The primary key of the created row, returned so that clients can retry
An API key scoped to a single operation that expires once it is used
questions.why: It is how payment APIs make "create a charge" safe to retry after a timeout: the server stores the key with the result and replays that result instead of charging twice. A body hash cannot tell a retry from a genuine second identical order.
questions.asked: A strong answer to "how do you stop a double charge?"

questions.q: Behind a reverse proxy, what is the difference between 502 and 503?
choices: 502: the upstream took too long; 503: the upstream returned invalid HTML
502: a proxy got a bad reply from upstream; 503: the service is refusing work
502: the app threw an unhandled exception; 503: the database is unreachable
502: the client sent a malformed request; 503: the DNS lookup failed
questions.why: 502 usually means the app behind the proxy is down or closed the connection; 503 is the app or load balancer declining work, often with Retry-After. A slow upstream is 504, and an unhandled exception in your app is a 500 that the proxy passes through.
questions.asked: Every on-call engineer has read these codes at 3am; knowing which layer each points at speeds up triage.

questions.q: A search on a collection matches nothing. What should the API return?
choices: 404, because nothing matched and the client should treat it as missing
204 No Content, since there are no items to put in a response body
200 with an empty array: the collection exists and simply has no items
400, because the filter was too narrow to match any of the rows
questions.why: 404 means the endpoint or resource does not exist; using it for an empty result forces every client to treat a normal case as an error. 204 breaks clients that always parse a JSON array. An empty list is a successful answer.
questions.asked: Tests whether you design for the client code that consumes the response.

questions.q: For a CRUD app, what is the practical trade-off between REST and GraphQL?
choices: GraphQL lets clients pick fields; REST keeps HTTP caching and the surface simple
GraphQL is faster in every case, since it always needs one round trip
REST cannot express relationships, so related data needs GraphQL to fetch
GraphQL replaces the data layer, so the server needs no ORM or SQL at all
questions.why: GraphQL solves over- and under-fetching for many different clients. It costs you URL-based HTTP caching, brings resolver N+1 risk, and needs query depth and cost limits. For one web client and a small team, REST is usually the right call.
questions.asked: An opinion question in disguise; naming the trade-offs matters more than the choice.

questions.q: Why does an internal-facing API still need rate limiting?
choices: To make billing simpler, since each request then costs a fixed amount
To cut log volume, since rejected requests are never written to logs
It does not: internal callers are trusted, so limits only add latency
So one buggy or hostile client cannot use up capacity for everyone
questions.why: Most rate-limit incidents are self-inflicted: a retry loop or a runaway batch job from a trusted service. A limit per caller turns "the whole API is down" into "one client gets 429s".
questions.asked: Checks you think of limits as capacity protection, not only as an anti-abuse feature.

questions.q: On a request, what do `Content-Type` and `Accept` each describe?
choices: They are one header, renamed between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
Content-Type describes the body sent; Accept, what you want back
Accept is set by servers; Content-Type is only set by clients
Content-Type belongs on responses; requests describe bodies with Accept
questions.why: Forgetting `Content-Type: application/json` on a POST is why the body goes missing: the JSON parser skips a type it does not match, so in Express 5 `req.body` stays undefined (Express 4 gave `{}`). Accept drives content negotiation for the response.
questions.asked: Basic, but it explains the most common "my body is empty" bug.

questions.q: A DELETE succeeds. What should it return?
choices: 201 Created, because the deletion is recorded as a new server event
404 Not Found, to confirm the resource no longer exists after the call
302 Found, redirecting the client to the collection it was removed from
204 No Content, or 200 with a body if there is something useful to say
questions.why: A second DELETE of the same id may return 204 (idempotent view) or 404 (literal view); both are defensible, so pick one and document it. The first, successful call should not look like a failure.
questions.asked: The second-DELETE follow-up tests whether you understand idempotency is about state, not status codes.

questions.q: What does HTTPS actually protect?
choices: The server itself from attacks, since only encrypted requests reach the app
Stored data too, since TLS also encrypts the rows at rest inside the database server
Against injection, since TLS rejects any request whose payload was altered
Confidentiality and integrity in transit, plus proof of the server's identity
questions.why: TLS stops interception and tampering between client and server, and the certificate proves who the server is. An attacker can send a perfectly encrypted injection payload; what you store, log or expose afterwards is outside TLS.
questions.asked: Checks you do not treat "we use HTTPS" as a security posture.

questions.q: Your endpoint takes 4 seconds because it calls three independent services in sequence. What is the cheapest fix that keeps the response the same?
choices: Put a cache in front of the endpoint so repeat calls skip all three
Call the three services concurrently instead of one after another
Raise the client timeout so the four seconds stop causing errors
Move the work to a background job and return 202 straight away
questions.why: Three 1.3 s calls in series take 4 s; concurrently they take about 1.3 s. A cache still pays full price on every miss, a longer timeout hides the latency, and 202 changes the contract the client depends on.
questions.asked: A practical latency question: the same lesson as the Promise.all question, at the service level.

questions.q: What is a webhook?
choices: The provider calls your endpoint when an event happens, instead of polling
A script the browser runs when the page receives a push notification
A long-lived WebSocket that the provider keeps open to your server
A scheduled job that fetches changes from the provider every minute
questions.why: Your endpoint must verify the signature, respond fast (do the work asynchronously) and tolerate duplicates, because providers retry until they get a 2xx. Fetching on a schedule is polling, the thing webhooks replace.
questions.asked: Every payment or SaaS integration uses them; the retries-mean-duplicates point is what interviewers want.

questions.q: How do you choose between WebSockets, server-sent events and polling?
choices: WebSockets for everything, since SSE and polling are legacy workarounds
SSE for chat, since it is two-way; WebSockets only for file uploads
Two-way and chatty: WebSocket; server-to-client: SSE; rare updates: polling
Polling for anything live, since WebSockets always fail behind load balancers
questions.why: WebSockets cost you connection state, reconnection logic and load-balancer configuration. SSE is one-way over plain HTTP with automatic reconnect, enough for notifications or a progress feed. Polling every 30 seconds is genuinely fine for many dashboards.
questions.asked: Checks you pick the cheapest tool that meets the need instead of defaulting to WebSockets.

questions.q: You move `POST /v1/orders` to `/v2/orders`. Which redirect makes clients repeat the POST, body included, at the new URL?
choices: 301 Moved Permanently, the standard code for any permanent move
302 Found, which tells clients to repeat the exact request elsewhere
308 Permanent Redirect, which requires the method and body be kept
303 See Other, which re-sends the original body to the new URL
questions.why: Clients, browsers included, may turn a POST into a GET on 301 and 302, and 303 means "now GET this" by definition. 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) forbid changing the method, so the body is re-sent.
questions.asked: A detail that bites during API migrations; it shows you have read the method-preservation rules.

questions.q: A client POSTs an XML body to an endpoint that only reads JSON. Which status names the problem precisely?
choices: 406 Not Acceptable, as the server cannot accept the media format it was sent
415 Unsupported Media Type, as the body's Content-Type is not supported
422 Unprocessable Content, as the XML is well-formed but unexpected
501 Not Implemented, as the server has no XML parser installed at all
questions.why: 415 is about the request body's Content-Type. 406 is the mirror image: the server cannot produce any format listed in the request's Accept header. The names invite the swap, which is exactly why interviewers ask. 501 means the method itself is unsupported.
questions.asked: A quick precision check on content negotiation vocabulary.

questions.q: `GET /report` returns JSON or CSV depending on the Accept header, and a CDN caches it. Which response header stops the CDN serving one format to clients that asked for the other?
choices: ETag, so that the CDN can tell the JSON body apart from the CSV body
Content-Type, which caches already fold into the cache key they use
Cache-Control: public, so the CDN re-checks the format on each request
Vary: Accept, so caches keep a separate copy per Accept header value
questions.why: A cache keys on the URL unless `Vary` names request headers that also change the response. Without it, the first client's format is served to everyone. The same applies to `Accept-Encoding` (compressed vs not) and `Accept-Language`; an ETag validates a copy, it does not select one.
questions.asked: Checks you understand how caches choose a stored response, which explains a whole class of CDN bugs.

questions.q: What is a client's `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br` header asking for?
choices: A compressed response body, which the server labels with Content-Encoding
A response in a character set other than UTF-8, such as br or gzip
Encryption of the body with one of the listed ciphers, on top of TLS
Chunked transfer, so the body arrives in pieces as soon as it is ready
questions.why: The server may compress with gzip or Brotli and says which in `Content-Encoding`; JSON and HTML typically shrink by 70% or more. Character sets travel in the `charset` parameter of Content-Type, and chunking is Transfer-Encoding.
questions.asked: A junior-level check that you know the free performance win and where it is configured.

questions.q: What does designing an API contract-first with OpenAPI buy a team?
choices: The server is generated in full, so no handlers are written by hand
Runtime validation becomes unnecessary, since the spec rejects bad input
The teams agree one spec early, then generate clients, mocks and tests
Versioning becomes unnecessary, since a spec guarantees compatibility
questions.why: Frontend and backend can work in parallel against the agreed spec, with typed clients and mock servers generated from it, and CI can diff the spec to catch breaking changes. Generators produce stubs, not business logic, and the server must still validate what it receives.
questions.asked: Common in teams with separate frontend and backend developers; checks you know what the spec is for.

questions.q: A bulk endpoint creates 100 items and 3 fail validation. Which response lets the client recover cleanly?
choices: 201, since most items were created and the client can re-fetch for gaps
400 listing the three errors, while the other 97 items remain created
A per-item result list with status and errors, so it retries only failures
500, since the batch did not fully complete and the client should resend all of it
questions.why: The client needs to know exactly which items succeeded. Return per-item results (200 or 207 Multi-Status with an entry per index), or make the batch atomic and reject all of it. A 400 while 97 rows exist lies about state, and "resend it all" creates duplicates unless creation is idempotent.
questions.asked: Checks you design the failure path of a batch, which is where imports and syncs go wrong.

questions.q: A client sends `DELETE /api/articles/9` to a route that only supports GET and PUT. Which response is correct?
choices: 404 Not Found, because no DELETE handler exists for that path
405 Method Not Allowed, with an `Allow: GET, PUT` header
400 Bad Request, because the method is invalid for this URI
501 Not Implemented, since the server does not support DELETE
questions.why: 405 says the resource exists but this method is not supported on it, and RFC 9110 requires an `Allow` header listing the methods that are. 404 would claim the resource is missing; 501 is for a method the server does not recognise at all, anywhere.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know the codes beyond the big five and the header that must travel with 405.

questions.q: An endpoint accepts a video for transcoding that takes several minutes. What should `POST /api/transcodes` return immediately?
choices: 200 OK with an empty body, and the client polls the list endpoint
201 Created with the finished video URL filled in as null for now
202 Accepted with a `Location` pointing at a job-status resource
204 No Content, because nothing is ready to send back to the client
questions.why: 202 means the request was accepted for processing that has not finished, and the job-status URL gives the client something to poll (or a webhook fires later). 201 promises the resource exists now, which is untrue while the transcode is still running.
questions.asked: Long-running work is common in CRUD apps; a strong answer describes the status resource and what it returns when the job completes.

questions.q: Which statement about 204 No Content is correct?
choices: It must not include a body, and clients should not try to parse one
It is only valid as a response to DELETE, never to PUT or PATCH
It tells the browser to clear the current page and show a blank one
It may carry a JSON body as long as `Content-Length` is set to zero
questions.why: A 204 has no content by definition, so a client that calls `res.json()` on it throws. It is valid for any method where there is nothing useful to return, commonly PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
questions.asked: Catches the frontend bug of calling `response.json()` unconditionally on a successful response.

questions.q: In the browser, what does this code log when the server responds 404 with a JSON error body?
choices: caught TypeError, since fetch rejects on any 4xx status
caught HTTPError, the error type fetch uses for 4xx/5xx
ok? false 404, because fetch only rejects on network failure
ok? true 404, because the server did send back a response
questions.why: `fetch` resolves for any HTTP response, including 404 and 500; it rejects (with a TypeError) only when no response arrives, such as a DNS failure, CORS block or abort. You must check `res.ok` (status 200–299) yourself.
questions.asked: The most common fetch bug in take-homes; a strong answer shows a wrapper that throws on `!res.ok`.

questions.q: A user requests `GET /api/posts/123`, but that post was deliberately and permanently removed. Which status tells clients and crawlers not to try again?
choices: 404 Not Found, the only code for a resource that is not there
410 Gone, meaning the resource existed and is permanently removed
301 Moved Permanently, pointing at the site's home page instead
403 Forbidden, because nobody may access the deleted post now
questions.why: 410 states the removal is intentional and permanent, so search engines drop the URL faster and clients can stop retrying. 404 makes no claim about permanence; redirecting deleted content to the home page is treated as a soft 404.
questions.asked: Shows awareness that status codes carry meaning for caches and crawlers, not just for your own frontend.

questions.q: A client uploads a 60 MB file to an endpoint whose limit is 10 MB. Which status fits best?
choices: 400 Bad Request, because the upload fails the endpoint's validation
413 Content Too Large, because the body exceeds what the server accepts
422 Unprocessable Content, because the file cannot be processed as sent
507 Insufficient Storage, because the server will not store that much
questions.why: 413 (renamed from 'Payload Too Large' in RFC 9110) names the exact problem, and proxies such as nginx emit it before your code even runs. 507 is a WebDAV code about the server running out of space, not a per-request limit.
questions.asked: Often asked alongside 'where do you enforce upload limits', where the answer is at the proxy and in the framework.

questions.q: What does `206 Partial Content` indicate?
choices: The server answered a `Range` request with only the requested bytes
The server timed out part-way and is sending what it had so far
The response was truncated because it exceeded the client's buffer
Only some items in a bulk request succeeded and the rest failed
questions.why: 206 answers a request with a `Range: bytes=...` header, returning a `Content-Range` slice; it is how video seeking and resumable downloads work. It is not a 'partial success' code for bulk operations, which is a common misuse.
questions.asked: Comes up when discussing file downloads or video; misusing 206 for bulk results is a red flag.

questions.q: Why does a 308 redirect exist when 301 already means 'moved permanently'?
choices: 308 can be cached by browsers, whereas a 301 can never be cached
308 is only for HTTPS upgrades, while 301 is for moved domains
308 forbids changing the method, while 301 lets a POST become GET
308 is the HTTP/2 version of 301, and HTTP/1.1 clients ignore it
questions.why: Historically browsers turned a redirected POST into a GET on 301 and 302, dropping the body. 307 and 308 were added so the method and body are preserved; both 301 and 308 are cacheable by default.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see if you understand why API redirects silently lose request bodies.

questions.q: A successful `PUT /api/settings` replaces the user's settings. Which response pairs are both correct?
choices: 201 with the new settings, or 202 if the write will happen later
200 with the stored representation, or 204 with no body at all
200 with `{ success: true }`, or 304 if nothing actually changed
204 with the stored settings, or 205 to make the client refresh
questions.why: Either return the updated representation with 200 (saving the client a GET) or return 204 with nothing. 201 applies only when the PUT created the resource; 304 is only for conditional GET/HEAD, never a write.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions returning the representation so the client sees server-set fields like `updatedAt`.

questions.q: Your API sits behind a load balancer. The upstream app takes 70 seconds and the balancer's timeout is 60. What does the client most likely receive?
choices: 500 Internal Server Error, raised by the app when the balancer disconnects
408 Request Timeout, because the client waited too long for its answer
503 Service Unavailable, because the balancer marks the app as down
504 Gateway Timeout, generated by the balancer, not by your own code
questions.why: 504 means a gateway or proxy did not get a timely response from upstream. 408 is sent by a server when the client was too slow to send its request, which is the opposite direction.
questions.asked: Debugging 502/504 in production is a mid-level expectation; strong answers mention that your app logs may show nothing.

questions.q: A client sends `Accept: application/xml` to an endpoint that can only produce JSON. What are the reasonable responses?
choices: 406 Not Acceptable, or ignore the header and send JSON anyway
415 Unsupported Media Type, since XML is not a type the API reads
400 Bad Request, because an XML Accept header is not valid here
200 with an empty body, because nothing matching could be made
questions.why: RFC 9110 allows either a 406 or disregarding `Accept` and sending the default representation; many APIs choose the latter. 415 is about the request body's `Content-Type`, not what the client wants back.
questions.asked: Pairs with the 406-vs-415 distinction, which reveals whether you know which header each code is about.

questions.q: What is the difference between a safe method and an idempotent one?
choices: Safe methods need authentication; idempotent ones can run anonymously
Safe means read-only in intent; idempotent means repeats give one end state
Safe methods are cached by browsers; idempotent ones are cached by proxies
Safe means it cannot fail; idempotent means it always returns the same body
questions.why: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are safe: the client is not asking for a state change. PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe. Idempotency is about server state, not identical responses; a second DELETE can return 404.
questions.asked: Standard warm-up; a strong answer gives an example of a method that is idempotent but not safe.

questions.q: What is a HEAD request typically used for?
choices: Sending only headers to the server, with the request body stripped
Fetching the first part of a resource before streaming the rest
Getting the headers a GET would return, such as size, with no body
Asking the server which HTTP methods a given resource supports
questions.why: HEAD returns the same status and headers as GET without the body, so a client can check existence, `Content-Length`, `ETag` or `Last-Modified` cheaply. Listing supported methods is what OPTIONS (or the `Allow` header) is for.
questions.asked: Link checkers and download managers rely on it; it tests breadth beyond GET and POST.

questions.q: Is it valid for a `GET` request to carry a JSON body with search filters?
choices: Yes, and every server and proxy is required to forward and read it
Yes, HTTP/2 made GET bodies standard, so it is now the preferred style
No, fetch sends it but servers must reply 400 to any GET with a body
It has no defined meaning, so proxies, caches and fetch may drop or reject it
questions.why: RFC 9110 says a body on GET has no generally defined semantics; the browser's `fetch` throws if you pass one, and caches key on the URL only. Put filters in the query string, or use POST (or the newer QUERY method draft) for large searches.
questions.asked: Comes up when designing complex search; a strong answer mentions POST-for-search and its caching trade-off.

questions.q: A POST to `/api/login` gets a 302 redirect to `/dashboard`. What does the browser do next?
choices: It re-sends the POST, login body included, to `/dashboard`
It issues a GET to `/dashboard` and drops the request body
It prompts the user to confirm re-sending the form data
It stops, because a redirect is not allowed after a POST
questions.why: For 301, 302 and 303, browsers switch a POST to a GET without a body; 303 See Other makes that explicit and is the textbook Post/Redirect/Get code. Only 307 and 308 re-send the POST.
questions.asked: Leads into the Post/Redirect/Get pattern that stops refresh from resubmitting forms.

questions.q: What is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern for server-rendered forms?
choices: Redirecting every POST through a CDN so the response is cached
Answering a successful form POST with 303 to a page the browser GETs
Converting forms to GET so that their submissions can be bookmarked
Having the browser GET a CSRF token before each POST it submits
questions.why: After a successful POST the server replies 303 See Other; the browser loads the result page with GET, so refresh or back does not resubmit the form and create a duplicate. It is a UX and duplicate-prevention pattern, not a caching or CSRF one.
questions.asked: Still asked for MVC and Razor Pages roles; a strong answer names the duplicate-submission problem it solves.

questions.q: Which part of this URL is never sent to the server? `https://shop.example/products?id=7#reviews`
choices: The fragment `#reviews`, which stays inside the browser
The query string `?id=7`, which only JavaScript can read
The scheme `https`, since the connection already implies it
The host `shop.example`, as it only resolves the IP address
questions.why: The fragment is client-side only: it scrolls to an anchor or drives client routing, and never appears in the request line or server logs. The host is sent in the `Host` header (or `:authority` in HTTP/2) and the query string is part of the request target.
questions.asked: Explains why hash-based routers need no server config and why tokens in fragments do not reach server logs.

questions.q: A search term `rock & roll` must go into a query string. What does this Node 24 code print?
choices: ?q=rock & roll
?q=rock%20%26%20roll
?q=rock+%26+roll
?q=rock+&+roll
questions.why: `URLSearchParams` uses form encoding, so spaces become `+` and `&` becomes `%26`. Building query strings by string concatenation would leave the raw `&`, splitting the value into a second parameter.
questions.asked: Tests whether you build URLs with the platform API instead of concatenation, a real source of bugs.

questions.q: What does the `Host` header do in an HTTP/1.1 request?
choices: It tells the server the client's hostname for logging purposes
It names the site requested, so one IP can serve many domains
It chooses which backend in a cluster should handle the request
It is optional metadata that proxies add and origin servers ignore
questions.why: `Host` is mandatory in HTTP/1.1 and enables virtual hosting: many domains on one IP and port, with the server routing by header. TLS uses SNI for the same purpose before any HTTP is exchanged.
questions.asked: Warm-up question that leads into reverse proxies, SNI and multi-tenant hosting.

questions.q: Behind a reverse proxy, your Express app logs every request as coming from `10.0.0.5`. What is the correct fix?
choices: Read the first IP in `X-Forwarded-For` without any further checks
Use `req.socket.remoteAddress`, which always holds the real client
Set `trust proxy` to the proxy hop so `req.ip` reads forwarded headers
Ask the proxy to rewrite the TCP source address to the client's IP
questions.why: The socket address is the proxy's. Express's `trust proxy` setting tells it how many hops to trust when deriving `req.ip` from `X-Forwarded-For`; blindly taking the first entry lets any client spoof its IP by sending the header itself, which breaks rate limiting.
questions.asked: Real production bug; a strong answer mentions IP spoofing and ASP.NET Core's ForwardedHeaders middleware equivalent.

questions.q: What does `Content-Length` tell the recipient, and what replaces it when the size is unknown up front?
choices: The body size in bytes; chunked transfer or HTTP/2 framing replaces it
The body size in characters; `Content-Range` replaces it for streams
The maximum size allowed; `Accept-Ranges` replaces it for large files
The compressed size in kilobytes; `Content-Encoding` replaces it for gzip
questions.why: `Content-Length` is a byte count, which matters for UTF-8 where characters are multi-byte. When a server streams a response of unknown length, HTTP/1.1 uses `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, while HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 mark the end with frames.
questions.asked: Shows up when debugging streamed responses or a mismatched length that hangs the client.

questions.q: Your API returns a JSON body in reply to a HEAD request, and it passes local tests. Why is that wrong?
choices: HEAD must return 204, so any body produces a protocol error
HEAD responses never have a body, so clients ignore or misread it
HEAD is only for CORS checks, so the body leaks data cross-origin
HEAD bodies are allowed but must be sent as plain text, not JSON
questions.why: A HEAD response carries GET's headers, including `Content-Length`, but no body; a body can desync a keep-alive connection. Most frameworks (Express, ASP.NET Core) handle HEAD by running the GET handler and discarding the body for you.

questions.q: What does an `OPTIONS` request with no CORS headers ask a server?
choices: To return the resource's metadata without authenticating the caller
To list which communication options, such as methods, the target supports
To return the cached copy of the resource with any options applied
To confirm the server is healthy before the client sends a real request
questions.why: OPTIONS asks about the capabilities of the target resource, typically answered with an `Allow` header. CORS preflights reuse the method with extra `Access-Control-Request-*` headers, which is why many devs only know it from CORS.
questions.asked: Probes whether you know OPTIONS predates CORS, which helps when a framework's routing rejects preflights.

questions.q: A proxy returns 502 Bad Gateway. What does that tell you about the upstream app?
choices: It replied too slowly, so the proxy gave up waiting on it
It returned a well-formed 500 that the proxy passed along
It sent an invalid response, or the connection to it failed
It is in maintenance mode and has asked the proxy to back off
questions.why: 502 means the gateway got an invalid response from upstream, which in practice includes a refused or reset connection (app crashed, wrong port). Slowness is 504; a deliberate 'not now' is 503; a 500 from the app is forwarded as 500.
questions.asked: Reading 502 versus 504 correctly tells you whether to look at crashes or slowness, which interviewers probe for on-call experience.

questions.q: An API returns `200 OK` with `{ "error": "Invalid email" }` for failed validation. What concretely goes wrong?
choices: Browsers refuse to parse JSON from a 200 that contains an `error` key
Nothing, as long as the frontend always checks for the `error` field
The response becomes uncacheable because it contains error content
Clients, retries, monitoring and caches all treat the failure as success
questions.why: Status codes are how generic tooling understands outcomes: `res.ok` is true, error-rate dashboards stay green, a CDN may even cache the error. Every consumer then has to know your private convention.
questions.asked: Classic code-review finding; a strong answer lists the concrete tools that get fooled.

questions.q: A client has been sending requests to your API for a year. You rename `GET /api/customers` to `/api/clients`. What keeps old clients working with least effort?
choices: Return 410 Gone from the old path so clients notice and update
Return 308 from the old path to the new one and keep it for a period
Return 404 from the old path and publish a changelog with the rename
Return 303 from the old path so that clients switch to a GET request
questions.why: A permanent, method-preserving redirect keeps GETs and any writes working while clients migrate, though many HTTP clients do not follow redirects for non-GET methods, so announce the change too. 410 and 404 break every existing client immediately.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about existing consumers before renaming anything in a public API.

questions.q: What does `Retry-After` mean on a 503 response?
choices: How long the server estimates it will be unavailable before retrying
The number of retries the client is allowed before being banned
The minimum wait between any two requests during normal operation
The time at which the server's cache for this resource expires
questions.why: On 503 (and 429, and 3xx) `Retry-After` gives either a number of seconds or an HTTP date. Well-behaved clients honour it rather than retrying immediately, which would keep an overloaded server down.
questions.asked: Follows naturally from 429; strong answers link it to backoff and thundering-herd problems.

questions.q: Which status should a login endpoint return when the email and password do not match?
choices: 403 Forbidden, because the credentials presented are not permitted
404 Not Found when the email is unknown, and 401 for a bad password
400 Bad Request, because the body contained invalid credentials
401 Unauthorized, with the same message whether email or password is wrong
questions.why: Authentication failed, so 401; the identical message stops attackers enumerating which emails have accounts. Returning 404 for unknown emails is exactly that enumeration leak. Some APIs use 400 for form logins, but never with distinguishable messages.
questions.asked: Combines status codes with account enumeration, a favourite security follow-up.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between HTTP/2 and HTTP/3?
choices: HTTP/3 adds server push, which HTTP/2 never supported in browsers
HTTP/3 replaces JSON with binary encoding for request payloads
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, so one lost packet stalls only its stream
HTTP/3 drops TLS for speed, relying on QUIC's own checksums instead
questions.why: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, so a lost packet stalls every stream (TCP head-of-line blocking). QUIC gives each stream independent delivery and integrates TLS 1.3, with faster connection setup. Server push was removed from browsers, not added.
questions.asked: Asked in performance-leaning interviews; strong answers mention it is enabled at the CDN or proxy, not in app code.

questions.q: Why is domain sharding (spreading assets over `static1`, `static2` hosts) now considered an anti-pattern?
choices: Browsers block pages that load assets from more than one subdomain
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection per origin
CDNs charge per hostname, so extra domains raise bandwidth costs
Cookies are always sent to every subdomain, doubling request size
questions.why: Sharding worked around HTTP/1.1's roughly six connections per host. With HTTP/2 one connection carries everything, and extra hosts cost DNS lookups and TLS handshakes while defeating prioritisation.

questions.q: A fingerprinted bundle `app.3f9c2a.js` never changes at that URL. Which `Cache-Control` value suits it?
choices: `no-cache`, so the browser checks with the server on every load
`public, max-age=31536000, immutable`
`private, max-age=60, must-revalidate` so updates show up quickly
`no-store`, so a stale bundle can never be served after a deploy
questions.why: A content hash in the filename means a new build gets a new URL, so the old one can be cached for a year and `immutable` stops even reload revalidation. The HTML that references the bundle is what must stay short-lived or `no-cache`.
questions.asked: The standard 'how do you cache a SPA' question; strong answers contrast the hashed assets with index.html.

questions.q: After every deploy, some users get a blank SPA page until they hard-refresh. What caching mistake is the most likely cause?
choices: The hashed JS bundles were served with a max-age of one year
The CDN was set to compress JS with Brotli instead of gzip
`index.html` is cached long-term and still names deleted bundles
The API responses were sent with `Cache-Control: no-store`
questions.why: A stale `index.html` references old hashed bundles that the deploy removed, so the script 404s and nothing renders. Serve the HTML with `no-cache` (revalidate every time) and keep old bundles around briefly across deploys.
questions.asked: A real incident shape; a strong answer includes keeping the previous build's assets on the CDN.

questions.q: What does `s-maxage` do that `max-age` does not?
choices: It sets a lifetime for shared caches like CDNs, overriding `max-age` there
It sets the lifetime in seconds, whereas `max-age` is measured in minutes
It applies only to secure HTTPS responses, while `max-age` covers plain HTTP
It limits how long a stale response may be served while revalidating
questions.why: `s-maxage` applies only to shared caches, so `max-age=0, s-maxage=300` lets a CDN hold a page for five minutes while browsers always revalidate. The stale-serving window is `stale-while-revalidate`.
questions.asked: Separates people who have configured a CDN from those who have only read about browser caching.

questions.q: A response with `Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` is 120 seconds old. What happens on the next request?
choices: The cache blocks the request until it has fetched a fresh copy
The cache serves the stale copy at once and refreshes in the background
The cache discards the entry and returns a 504 to the client
The cache serves the copy only if the origin is currently down
questions.why: Within the 300-second window after going stale, the cache may return the stale response immediately and revalidate asynchronously, hiding origin latency. Serving stale only when the origin is failing is `stale-if-error`.
questions.asked: Shows up in CDN and SWR (the React library is named after it) discussions; strong answers name the latency trade-off.

questions.q: The browser sends `If-None-Match: "v7"` and the resource's current ETag is still `"v7"`. What should the server send?
choices: 200 with the full body, plus the same ETag header again
412 Precondition Failed, because that tag has already been sent before
304 Not Modified with no body, so the cached copy is reused
204 No Content, because there is nothing new to send back
questions.why: A matching `If-None-Match` on a GET means the client's copy is current, so the server answers 304 with no body and the browser uses its cache. 412 is for failed preconditions on writes such as `If-Match`.
questions.asked: Basic conditional GET; follow-ups ask what the server saves (bandwidth, sometimes not the database query).

questions.q: What is the difference between a strong ETag `"abc"` and a weak one `W/"abc"`?
choices: Weak tags expire after one hour; strong ones last until the resource changes
Weak tags are for GET only; strong tags are required for PUT and DELETE
Strong means byte-identical; weak means semantically equivalent content
Strong tags are hashed with SHA-256; weak ones may use MD5 or CRC32
questions.why: A strong validator changes whenever any byte changes, so it is safe for range requests and `If-Match`; a weak one only promises equivalent meaning, which suits responses that differ by compression or whitespace. Neither implies a hash algorithm or lifetime.
questions.asked: Comes up when a proxy's gzip turns ETags weak and If-Match writes start failing.

questions.q: How does an ETag help prevent lost updates when two users edit the same record?
choices: The server locks the row while any client holds the current ETag
The client sends `If-Match` with its ETag, and a stale one gets 412
The client sends `If-None-Match`, and the server merges both edits
The CDN rejects the second PUT because its ETag is already cached
questions.why: Optimistic concurrency: the PUT carries `If-Match: "v7"`; if someone else saved first the ETag is now `"v8"`, so the server refuses with 412 Precondition Failed and the client refetches. No lock is held while a user edits.
questions.asked: Strong answers map it to a rowversion or version column in EF Core, the database side of the same idea.

questions.q: An API wants to force clients to use `If-Match` on every PUT so no client can blindly overwrite. Which status rejects a PUT that omits it?
choices: 409 Conflict
412 Precondition Failed
428 Precondition Required
400 Bad Request with a note
questions.why: 428 (RFC 6585) means the server requires the request to be conditional. 412 is for a precondition that was sent but failed; 409 describes a state conflict, not a missing header.

questions.q: Why does a CDN caching `GET /api/me` without care risk a data leak?
choices: The CDN may serve one user's cached profile to the next user
The CDN strips the `Authorization` header before forwarding it
CDNs always cache 401 responses, locking out logged-in users
CDNs decompress JSON, which exposes it to other CDN tenants
questions.why: Unless the response is marked `private` or `no-store` (or the CDN is configured to bypass authenticated requests), a shared cache keyed by URL can hand the first user's data to everyone. Most CDNs skip caching when `Authorization` is present, but cookies are not always treated the same way.
questions.asked: A real incident class; strong answers mention `Cache-Control: private` as the explicit fix.

questions.q: What does `Cache-Control: private, max-age=300` allow?
choices: Any cache may store it, but only for the user who first requested it
The browser may cache it for five minutes; shared caches must not
Nobody may cache it, and `max-age` is ignored when `private` is set
The CDN may cache it for five minutes if the request used HTTPS
questions.why: `private` restricts storage to a single-user cache such as the browser, so per-user responses can still be cached locally. It is not encryption and does not stop the browser cache.

questions.q: A browser gets `Last-Modified: Tue, 02 Sep 2025 10:00:00 GMT` and no other caching headers. What may it do?
choices: It must revalidate on every request, as if `no-cache` were set
It must not cache the response, because no `max-age` was given
It caches it for exactly 24 hours, the HTTP default freshness
It may compute a heuristic freshness lifetime and reuse it unchecked
questions.why: Without explicit freshness, RFC 9111 lets caches use a heuristic, commonly 10% of the time since `Last-Modified`. That is why users sometimes see stale files: always set `Cache-Control` explicitly.
questions.asked: Explains a confusing 'why is this stale' bug; strong answers say never rely on heuristic caching.

questions.q: Why is `Vary: Accept-Encoding` sent with compressed responses?
choices: It tells the browser which compression algorithms the server supports
It makes caches store gzip and uncompressed copies as separate entries
It forces the browser to decompress the body before storing it
It stops proxies from recompressing a body that has already been compressed
questions.why: `Vary` lists request headers that change the response, so a cache keys on them too. Without it a proxy could hand a Brotli body to a client that cannot decode it.

questions.q: A CDN caches pages with `Vary: User-Agent`. What is the problem?
choices: The CDN will ignore the header and cache one copy for all browsers
Mobile browsers do not send a User-Agent, so they receive errors
Thousands of distinct UA strings split the cache, so hit rates collapse
`Vary` only accepts `Accept-*` headers, so the response is rejected
questions.why: Every UA string variant becomes a separate cache key, so almost nothing is ever reused. Normalise at the edge (for example to a device-class header) or avoid varying on UA at all.
questions.asked: Shows you understand that every `Vary` header multiplies cache keys, a lesson usually learned from a bad hit rate.

questions.q: In an ASP.NET Core 9 API, what is the key difference between response caching middleware and output caching middleware?
choices: Response caching stores in Redis; output caching can only use memory
Response caching obeys client headers; output caching is server-controlled
Output caching is for Razor views only; response caching covers APIs
Output caching sets `Cache-Control`; response caching stores the body
questions.why: Response caching follows HTTP caching rules, so a client sending `Cache-Control: no-cache` bypasses it. Output caching (`AddOutputCache`) is configured on the server, ignores client cache headers, supports tag-based eviction and can use Redis.
questions.asked: Asked in .NET roles; the strong answer is why output caching is the one you usually want for APIs.

questions.q: A React app on `https://app.example` calls `https://api.example`. Which statement is true?
choices: They share an origin because the registrable domain is the same
They are different origins, so the API must answer with CORS headers
They share an origin because both use HTTPS on the default port 443
Only cookies differ between them; fetch calls are unaffected by CORS
questions.why: An origin is scheme + host + port, and `app.` and `api.` are different hosts. They are, however, the same site, which matters for `SameSite` cookies; same-site and same-origin are not the same thing.
questions.asked: The origin-versus-site distinction is a common follow-up that exposes how deep the candidate's model goes.

questions.q: Which cross-origin request is sent without a preflight?
choices: A PUT with `Content-Type: application/json` and no custom headers
A GET with an `Authorization: Bearer` header
A POST with `Content-Type: text/plain` and no custom headers
A DELETE with no body and no extra request headers set
questions.why: Simple requests are GET, HEAD or POST with only safelisted headers and a form-like content type (`text/plain`, `multipart/form-data`, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`). `Authorization`, JSON content type, PUT and DELETE all trigger a preflight.
questions.asked: Explains why adding a JSON header suddenly makes 'CORS break'; strong answers link simple requests to CSRF.

questions.q: A cross-origin fetch fails with a CORS error, but the server log shows the request ran and a row was inserted. How is that possible?
choices: The browser retried the request, and the retry succeeded silently
CORS blocks JavaScript from reading the response, not from sending it
The server ran the preflight OPTIONS as if it were the actual POST
The log is wrong, since CORS stops the request leaving the browser
questions.why: For simple requests the browser sends the request and only withholds the response from your code if CORS headers are missing. That is why CORS is not a defence against CSRF: side effects still happen.
questions.asked: Strong answers conclude that server-side authorization and CSRF protection must not depend on CORS.

questions.q: A cross-origin fetch uses `credentials: 'include'`. Which response header setup lets the browser expose the response?
choices: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Allow-Credentials: true`
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example` plus `Allow-Credentials: true`
`Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` alone, as the origin is implied
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alone, since the cookie is on the request
questions.why: With credentials the wildcard is forbidden; the server must echo the exact origin and send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Echoing any origin without an allowlist check is a serious misconfiguration.
questions.asked: Cookie-based SPAs on a separate API domain hit this immediately, so it reveals hands-on CORS debugging.

questions.q: Your API reflects the request's `Origin` into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for an allowlist of three sites, and a CDN caches responses. Which header must you also send?
choices: `Vary: Origin`, so each origin gets its own cached response
`Access-Control-Max-Age`, so the CDN knows how long to cache
`Cache-Control: public`, so the CDN can store all the variants
`Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Origin` for the browser to see it
questions.why: Without `Vary: Origin`, the CDN may serve a response carrying site A's allowed origin to site B, whose browser then blocks it. The cors middleware packages add `Vary: Origin` for you when reflecting origins.
questions.asked: Intermittent 'CORS works for some users' bugs come from this; it shows real debugging experience.

questions.q: What does `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600` on a preflight response do?
choices: It lets the browser cache the preflight result for up to 600 seconds
It lets the actual response be cached by the browser for 600 seconds
It limits the cross-origin session to 600 seconds before re-login
It tells the server to reject preflights sent more than 600s apart
questions.why: The browser can skip repeat OPTIONS requests for the same URL, method and headers while the cached preflight is valid; browsers cap the value (Chromium at two hours). It has no effect on caching the real response.

questions.q: Your frontend needs to read a custom `X-Total-Count` header from a cross-origin response, but `res.headers.get()` returns null. What fixes it?
choices: Sending `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: X-Total-Count` on the preflight
Adding `Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Total-Count` to the response
Setting `mode: 'no-cors'` on the fetch so all headers become readable
Renaming it to `Total-Count`, since `X-` headers are always hidden
questions.why: Cross-origin JavaScript can read only CORS-safelisted response headers unless the server exposes others. `Allow-Headers` is the opposite direction (request headers the client may send), and `no-cors` gives an opaque response with nothing readable.
questions.asked: A very common pagination bug; mixing up Allow-Headers and Expose-Headers is the tell.

questions.q: In development, a Vite React app on port 5173 calls an API on port 5000 and hits CORS errors. What avoids CORS entirely for local development?
choices: Setting `mode: 'no-cors'` on every fetch call the app makes
Running the browser with web security disabled during development
Configuring Vite's dev server to proxy `/api` to the backend
Moving the API to port 80 so the ports no longer need to match
questions.why: With a dev-server proxy the browser only talks to its own origin, and Vite forwards `/api` server-side, where CORS does not apply. Production can mirror this with a reverse proxy serving both on one origin.
questions.asked: Practical question; a strong answer mentions serving SPA and API from one origin in production too.

questions.q: A request arrives with `Accept: application/json;q=0.5, text/csv`. Which format does the client prefer?
choices: JSON, because it is listed first in the header
Either one; order and `q` values are only hints
CSV, because it has the implicit quality of 1
JSON, because `q=0.5` marks it as the default
questions.why: Each media range has a quality value from 0 to 1, defaulting to 1 when omitted; higher wins regardless of order. So `text/csv` (q=1) beats JSON (q=0.5).
questions.asked: Checks that you can read q-values rather than assuming header order decides preference.

questions.q: What does `Accept-Language: fr-CA, fr;q=0.8, en;q=0.5` let an API do?
choices: Force the browser to translate the JSON response client-side
Pick the best localised representation the server can produce
Reject clients whose preferred language the server lacks with 406
Set the response's `Content-Type` charset to a French encoding
questions.why: It is proactive content negotiation: the server chooses among available translations and should reply with `Content-Language` and `Vary: Accept-Language`. Many apps prefer an explicit user setting, since browser language is often wrong for the user.

questions.q: A client sends a gzip-compressed request body. Which header tells the server how to decode it?
choices: `Accept-Encoding: gzip` on the request
`Content-Type: application/gzip`
`Transfer-Encoding: gzip` on the request
`Content-Encoding: gzip` on the request
questions.why: `Content-Encoding` describes how the body being sent is encoded, in either direction; `Accept-Encoding` only states what the sender can receive. Servers often reject compressed request bodies unless configured, partly because of zip-bomb risk.

questions.q: Why should you not gzip a response that contains both a secret CSRF token and text the attacker can inject, over HTTPS?
choices: Gzip breaks the TLS record layer, so responses arrive corrupted
Gzip exposes the plain text to any proxy between the two ends
Compressed size leaks guesses about the secret (BREACH attack)
Gzip disables HTTP/2 multiplexing for that entire connection
questions.why: BREACH: when attacker-controlled input and a secret share a compressed response, the ciphertext length shrinks when the guess matches part of the secret. Mitigations include masking tokens per response, separating secrets from reflected input, or disabling compression for such pages.

questions.q: A client requests `Range: bytes=0-1023` on a large file. Which response headers accompany the 206?
choices: `Content-Range: bytes 0-1023/5000000` and `Content-Length: 1024`
`Accept-Ranges: 1024` and `Content-Length: 5000000` for the file
`Range: bytes 0-1023` echoed back and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`
`Content-Range: 1024` and `Content-Length: 5000000` for the file
questions.why: `Content-Range` states which bytes are included and the total size; `Content-Length` is the size of this part. `Accept-Ranges: bytes` in normal responses advertises that range requests are supported.

questions.q: What is the main reason API responses are usually served with `Cache-Control: no-store` or `private, no-cache` by default?
choices: Browsers cannot cache JSON, so any other value is simply ignored
API data is often per-user or changes often, so reuse is risky
HTTP/2 disables caching for requests that carry an `Authorization`
Setting any max-age on JSON breaks the browser's `fetch` API
questions.why: Browsers and CDNs can cache JSON perfectly well; the default is conservative because API data is usually user-specific or volatile. Public, rarely changing endpoints (a product catalogue) can and should use `max-age` plus ETags.
questions.asked: Checks that you choose cache headers per endpoint rather than blanket-disabling caching.

questions.q: Which of these responses does a shared cache store by default when no `Cache-Control` is present?
choices: A 200 to a GET, which can be heuristically cached
A 201 to a POST, which carries the new resource
A 500 to a GET, so a failing origin is shielded
A 302 to a GET, which is cached until the next redirect arrives
questions.why: 200 to GET is cacheable by default (as are 301, 308, 404, 410 and a few others), so heuristic freshness can apply. POST responses are only cacheable with explicit freshness, 5xx generally are not, and 302 is not cacheable by default.

questions.q: Which media type does RFC 9457 define for machine-readable HTTP error bodies?
choices: `application/problem+json`
`application/error+json` with a `code` field
`application/json` with a top-level `error` key
`text/problem` with a plain-text error message
questions.why: RFC 9457 (which obsoletes RFC 7807) defines Problem Details with members `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`, served as `application/problem+json`. ASP.NET Core emits it via `AddProblemDetails()` and `Results.Problem()`.
questions.asked: Knowing the standard by name signals you do not invent a new error format for every project.

questions.q: In an RFC 9457 problem details body, what is the `type` member for?
choices: The exception class name, such as `ValidationException`, for debugging
A URI identifying the kind of problem, stable enough for clients to switch on
The HTTP status family written as a word, such as `client-error` or `server-error`
The content type of the original request that caused the problem
questions.why: `type` is a URI (ideally dereferenceable to docs) naming the problem category, such as `https://api.example/problems/insufficient-funds`; clients branch on it rather than parsing `detail`. Exposing exception class names leaks internals. It defaults to `about:blank` when absent.
questions.asked: A strong answer contrasts `type` (for code) with `detail` (for humans) and mentions extension members.

questions.q: A form POST fails validation on two fields. How does an RFC 9457 response carry the per-field messages?
choices: In the `detail` string, as one sentence listing both fields
In two separate problem objects inside a top-level JSON array
In an extension member such as `errors` mapping field to messages
In response headers named after each field that failed validation
questions.why: Problem details allows extension members, and ASP.NET Core's `ValidationProblemDetails` uses `errors: { "email": ["..."] }`. A structured map lets the frontend put each message next to the right input; a sentence in `detail` cannot be mapped reliably.
questions.asked: Links API design to form UX; strong answers mention the field path format for nested objects.

questions.q: What should a 500 response body contain in production?
choices: A generic message plus a correlation id the user can quote to support
The exception message and stack trace so clients can report the bug
The failing SQL statement, so the team can reproduce the query quickly
Nothing at all, because any body on a 500 is a security vulnerability
questions.why: Stack traces and SQL leak internals useful to attackers; the details belong in server logs, joined to the response by a trace or correlation id. An empty body is safe but leaves support with nothing to search for.
questions.asked: Strong answers mention that ASP.NET Core's developer exception page must only run in Development.

questions.q: Which URL design follows REST conventions for 'the comments on post 42'?
choices: `GET /getCommentsForPost?postId=42`
`GET /posts/42/comments`
`POST /comments/search` with `{ postId: 42 }`
`GET /comment/list/42`
questions.why: Resources are plural nouns and the method carries the verb; nesting expresses 'belongs to'. Keep nesting to one level: `/comments/7` is a better address for a single comment than `/posts/42/comments/7` when comment ids are globally unique.

questions.q: How should a REST API model 'publish this draft article', an action that is not simple CRUD?
choices: `GET /articles/7/publish`, so that it can be triggered by a link
`PATCH /articles/7` with `{ status: "published" }` when it is just a state change
`POST /publishArticle?id=7`, because actions that are not CRUD should always be verbs
`PUT /articles/7/publish` with an empty body that the server ignores
questions.why: If publishing is only a field change with validation, PATCH the state. If it triggers significant side effects (notify subscribers, schedule), a sub-resource such as `POST /articles/7/publication` is also accepted. A GET with side effects is the one clearly wrong option.
questions.asked: Tests pragmatism: strong candidates give both options and the reason to choose each.

questions.q: What does HATEOAS add to a REST response?
choices: A schema version so clients can validate the response structure
Links to related actions and resources, so clients follow URLs not build them
A signed hash of the body, so that the client can detect any tampering in transit
An expiry time telling the client when to fetch the resource again
questions.why: Hypermedia controls (for example `_links.cancel.href`) let the server advertise what the client can do next in the current state. Few JSON APIs go all the way, but including `next` links in pagination is a widely used piece of it.
questions.asked: Usually asked as 'is your API really RESTful'; a pragmatic answer beats a purist one.

questions.q: A client needs to delete 500 records. What is a sensible API shape?
choices: 500 parallel `DELETE /items/:id` calls from the browser in one burst
`GET /items/delete?ids=1,2,3,...` so the ids fit in a single request
`POST /items/bulk-delete` with the ids in the body and a per-id result
`DELETE /items` with no body, clearing the collection the user sees
questions.why: A bulk endpoint keeps it to one request with a bounded body, and per-id results tell the client which failed. A GET with side effects is unsafe, 500 parallel calls hammer the server and rate limits, and a body-less collection DELETE is terrifyingly broad.
questions.asked: Bulk operations come up in almost every admin-screen design question.

questions.q: Should a JSON API wrap every response as `{ "data": ... }`?
choices: It is a style choice, useful for adding `meta` or paging alongside the data
Yes, because browsers refuse to parse a bare JSON array returned from any cross-origin API
No, because an envelope breaks HTTP caching of JSON responses
Yes, and the status code should also be duplicated inside the envelope
questions.why: Envelopes help when you need `meta` (totals, cursors) next to the payload, and top-level objects are easier to extend than bare arrays. The old top-level array concern was a JSON hijacking issue in ancient browsers, not a parsing limit, and duplicating the status in the body is redundant.

questions.q: A `GET /orders` endpoint returns `createdAt`. Which format is safest for dates in a JSON API?
choices: A locale string like `24/09/2026 14:00` expressed in the server's own local time zone
Seconds since the epoch as a string, to avoid float precision loss
ISO 8601 in UTC, such as `2026-09-24T14:00:00Z`, formatted by the client
A JavaScript `Date` object, which `JSON.stringify` preserves as a type
questions.why: ISO 8601 with an explicit offset is unambiguous, sortable and parsed by every platform; formatting for display belongs in the UI. JSON has no date type, so `JSON.stringify` turns a `Date` into an ISO string and `JSON.parse` leaves it as a string.
questions.asked: Time zone bugs are a common interview war story; strong answers mention storing UTC and formatting late.

questions.q: What does this Node 24 code print?
choices: number 0
string Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT
questions.why: `Date.prototype.toJSON` produces an ISO string, and `JSON.parse` has no way to know it was a date, so it stays a string. Clients must convert explicitly (or validate with a schema that coerces), otherwise date methods fail at runtime.
questions.asked: Dates arriving as strings is a daily frontend bug; the interviewer wants to hear where you convert them.

questions.q: Why should an API send large numeric ids, such as 64-bit database keys, as strings in JSON?
choices: JSON cannot represent integers, only floating-point numbers
JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53, corrupting the id
String ids compress better with gzip than numeric ones do
Numeric ids are not allowed as values for `Content-Type: application/json`
questions.why: `JSON.parse` turns numbers into IEEE-754 doubles, which are exact only up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1). A Snowflake-style id like 1234567890123456789 silently changes, so APIs such as Twitter's send `id_str`.
questions.asked: Real cross-language bug between C# `long` and JavaScript; strong answers mention BigInt and string ids.

questions.q: What does this Node 24 code print?
choices: It throws a RangeError
questions.why: 9007199254740993 is 2^53 + 1, which a double cannot represent, so it rounds to 9007199254740992 with no error. This is why APIs serialise 64-bit ids as strings.

questions.q: A PATCH body is `{ "nickname": null }`. With JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) semantics, what happens?
choices: The `nickname` field is left unchanged, as null values are skipped
The `nickname` field is removed or cleared on the stored resource
The request is rejected, because null is not valid in a merge patch
Every field not in the body is also set to null on the resource
questions.why: In merge patch, a present key with `null` means delete that member, and absent keys mean leave alone. Your deserialiser must distinguish absent from null; plain C# DTOs map both to null unless you track which properties were supplied.
questions.asked: Asked to see if you have hit the absent-versus-null problem when implementing PATCH.

questions.q: What does a JSON Patch (RFC 6902) request body look like?
choices: A partial object whose fields overwrite the stored resource's fields
An array of operations such as `{ op: "replace", path: "/name", value: "x" }`
A diff in unified format generated from the old and new JSON text
A full copy of the resource, with each changed field marked by a `$set` operator key
questions.why: JSON Patch (`application/json-patch+json`) is a list of add/remove/replace/move/copy/test operations with JSON Pointer paths, which can edit array items precisely. The partial-object style is JSON Merge Patch (`application/merge-patch+json`).

questions.q: Which API change is backwards compatible for existing JSON clients?
choices: Renaming the `userName` response field to `username`
Adding an optional `nickname` field to the response
Making a previously optional request field required
Changing `price` from a number to a formatted string
questions.why: Adding response fields is safe for tolerant readers that ignore unknown properties. Renames, type changes and new required inputs all break existing callers. Strict clients that reject unknown fields are a reason to document the 'ignore unknown fields' rule.
questions.asked: The base of every versioning conversation; strong answers mention enum additions as a subtle break.

questions.q: Your API adds a new value `"refunded"` to the `status` enum in responses. Why can this still break clients?
choices: Clients with exhaustive switches or strict enum parsing fail on the new value
It cannot break anything, because adding data is always backwards compatible
JSON enums are positional, so every existing value shifts along by one index number
Browsers cache enum schemas and reject values not seen on first load
questions.why: A C# client deserialising into an enum, or a TypeScript switch that throws on unknown values, breaks on an unexpected member. Document that enums may grow and that clients must handle unknown values.
questions.asked: Separates candidates who have maintained a public API from those who have only designed one.

questions.q: What do the `Deprecation` and `Sunset` response headers communicate?
