choices: That the response came from a stale cache and is due to be refreshed
That the endpoint is deprecated, and the date after which it stops working
That the client's API key expires soon and must be rotated before then
That the server is going into scheduled maintenance at the stated time
questions.why: `Sunset` (RFC 8594) gives the date the resource is expected to become unresponsive and `Deprecation` (RFC 9745) marks it deprecated, often with a `Link` to migration docs. Clients and API gateways can alert on them before anything breaks.
questions.asked: Shows you know how to retire an endpoint gracefully instead of just deleting it.

questions.q: Which versioning strategy is easiest to test in a browser and route at a gateway?
choices: A custom media type such as `Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json`
A custom request header such as `Api-Version: 2`
A version in the URL path, such as `/v2/orders`
A version negotiated inside the JSON request body
questions.why: Path versions are visible, bookmarkable and trivially routed by proxies. Header and media-type versioning keep URLs stable and are arguably purer, but need tooling to test; versioning in the body cannot work for GET.

questions.q: What does an OpenAPI document describe?
choices: An HTTP API's paths, operations, parameters, schemas and auth schemes
The deployment topology of the API servers and the load balancers that sit in front
Rate-limit quotas and billing tiers for each consumer of the API
The database tables behind each endpoint and their foreign keys
questions.why: OpenAPI (3.1 is current) is a machine-readable contract of the HTTP surface, used to render docs, generate clients and validate requests. It deliberately says nothing about storage or infrastructure.

questions.q: A team keeps its OpenAPI spec in the repo and wants CI to stop accidental breaking changes. What does that check compare?
choices: The spec's YAML formatting against a linter's style rules only
The new spec against the last released one, flagging breaking diffs
The number of endpoints, failing the build when the count goes down
Response times recorded against the spec's documented latency goals
questions.why: Tools such as oasdiff compare two OpenAPI versions and classify changes, for example a removed field, a newly required parameter or a narrowed enum, as breaking. Linting (Spectral) enforces style but cannot tell you what changed since the last release.
questions.asked: Shows you treat the API contract as something CI protects, not just documentation.

questions.q: A team generates TypeScript types for its React app from the backend's OpenAPI spec. What does that catch?
choices: Every runtime shape mismatch, so response validation can be skipped
Compile-time drift when the contract changes and the frontend has not
Slow endpoints, because the generator measures each operation's latency
Authorization bugs, because each generated type encodes its user roles
questions.why: Regenerating types after a spec change makes the compiler flag every call site that no longer fits. Types still vanish at runtime, so if the server deviates from its own spec, only runtime validation or contract tests will notice.
questions.asked: Strong answers pair generated types with runtime validation such as Zod at the boundary.

questions.q: In GraphQL, what is the N+1 problem and the standard fix?
choices: Clients send N+1 queries for each page; persisted queries batch them into one request
Each nested field resolver queries the DB per parent; DataLoader batches them
The schema has N+1 types per table; code generation collapses them down
Each mutation triggers N+1 subscriptions; debouncing merges the events
questions.why: Resolving `posts { author }` naively runs one query for posts and one per post for its author. DataLoader collects keys within a tick and issues one `WHERE id IN (...)` query, caching per request.
questions.asked: The first GraphQL performance question most interviewers ask; naming DataLoader is the expected answer.

questions.q: Why is HTTP caching harder for a GraphQL API than for REST?
choices: GraphQL responses are binary, so CDNs cannot store them at all
Queries usually go as POSTs to one URL, so URL-keyed caches miss
GraphQL forbids `Cache-Control`, as every result must be live
GraphQL servers must disable ETags to support subscriptions
questions.why: One endpoint with the query in a POST body gives caches nothing to key on. Persisted queries sent via GET (a hash in the URL) restore CDN caching; client caches such as Apollo's normalise by id instead.

questions.q: A GraphQL request partly fails: one field's resolver throws. What does the client typically receive?
choices: HTTP 500 with no data, because any resolver error aborts the query
HTTP 200 with partial `data` and an `errors` array naming the path
HTTP 207 Multi-Status with one status code for each requested field
HTTP 400, because the query was invalid for that field's resolver
questions.why: GraphQL over HTTP commonly returns 200 with `data` (the failed field null) plus `errors` with a `path`. Monitoring that only counts 5xx misses these failures, so GraphQL services track errors inside the body.
questions.asked: Monitoring GraphQL correctly needs this, and REST-only candidates rarely know it.

questions.q: What is the main reason teams pick gRPC for service-to-service calls?
choices: Browsers can call it directly with fetch and no proxy in the middle
A Protobuf contract generates typed clients, over efficient HTTP/2
It needs no schema, so services can evolve without coordinating
It returns JSON by default, making responses easy to read in logs
questions.why: gRPC uses `.proto` contracts to generate strongly typed clients and servers, sends compact binary messages, and supports streaming over HTTP/2. Browsers cannot speak raw gRPC, so they need gRPC-Web or Connect through a proxy.
questions.asked: Strong answers say REST stays the default for public and browser-facing APIs.

questions.q: In a Protobuf message used by gRPC, why must you never reuse a removed field's number?
choices: Field numbers identify data on the wire, so old clients would misread it
Protobuf assigns numbers alphabetically, so reuse reorders every field
Reused numbers make the generated C# class fail to compile at all
gRPC caches field numbers per connection and rejects any message whose numbers changed
questions.why: The binary encoding carries field numbers, not names; if 3 used to be `email` and now means `phone`, an old client decodes phone numbers as emails. Mark removed numbers `reserved` so the compiler blocks reuse.

questions.q: How do server-sent events (SSE) differ from WebSockets?
choices: SSE is one-way server to client over plain HTTP, with automatic reconnect
SSE is bidirectional but limited to binary frames rather than text
SSE needs a special protocol upgrade handshake, which most corporate proxies block outright
SSE only works over HTTP/1.1 and fails on HTTP/2 connections
questions.why: SSE is a long-lived `text/event-stream` response consumed by `EventSource`, which reconnects and can resume with `Last-Event-ID`. It is text-only and one-way; WebSockets are bidirectional and need an upgrade. SSE works well over HTTP/2.

questions.q: A long-lived SSE stream through nginx arrives at the browser in big delayed bursts. What is the usual cause?
choices: The browser's `EventSource` batches events every thirty seconds
HTTP/2 multiplexing merges events from different streams together
The proxy buffers the response; disable buffering for that route
Gzip cannot compress `text/event-stream`, so the proxy stalls it
questions.why: Reverse proxies buffer upstream responses by default; for streams you disable it (nginx `proxy_buffering off` or the `X-Accel-Buffering: no` response header) and make sure compression middleware flushes.

questions.q: Why is `POST /api/users/42/delete` a poor design compared with `DELETE /api/users/42`?
choices: It hides a delete behind a non-idempotent method, so tools cannot reason about it
Browsers refuse to send POST requests to any URL ending with a verb
A POST cannot carry authentication headers, so the delete ends up completely unprotected
A POST response is always cached by CDNs, so the delete would run once
questions.why: Using the right method lets clients, gateways and retry logic know the operation is idempotent and destructive, and keeps URLs as nouns. HTML forms only support GET and POST, which is where the verb-URL habit comes from.

questions.q: A React component fetches search results and must give up after 5 seconds. Which Node 24 / modern browser API does that most directly?
choices: `fetch(url, { timeout: 5000 })`, the built-in fetch timeout option
`fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })`
`Promise.race` with a `setTimeout`, which also cancels the request
`fetch(url, { keepalive: false })`, which closes idle connections
questions.why: `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` aborts the request and rejects with a `TimeoutError` DOMException. `fetch` has no `timeout` option, and `Promise.race` stops you waiting but leaves the request running.
questions.asked: Every HTTP client needs a timeout; strong answers also combine it with a user-cancel signal via `AbortSignal.any`.

questions.q: What does this Node 24 code print when the request is aborted by the timeout?
choices: AbortError
TimeoutError
TypeError
FetchError
questions.why: A signal from `AbortSignal.timeout` rejects with a DOMException named `TimeoutError`, whereas a manual `controller.abort()` gives `AbortError`. Distinguishing them lets you show 'timed out, retry?' rather than silently ignoring a user cancel.

questions.q: Where should a 201 response to `POST /api/invoices` point the client to find the new invoice?
choices: In a `Content-Location` header naming the collection URL
In a `Location` header with the new invoice's URL
In a `Link` header with `rel="self"` pointing at the POST URL
In a `Refresh` header that tells the browser to reload it
questions.why: `Location` on a 201 identifies the created resource; ASP.NET Core's `CreatedAtAction`/`Results.Created` and a manual `res.location()` in Express set it. Returning the body too saves the client a round trip.
questions.asked: A basic REST hygiene check that often appears in take-home code reviews.

questions.q: How does a JSON API commonly expose 'next page' links without an envelope, for example GitHub's API?
choices: A `Next-Page` custom header containing the next page number
A `Link` header with URLs tagged `rel="next"`, `rel="prev"` and so on
A `Location` header on every 200 response pointing at the next page
A `Refresh` header that makes the client fetch the next page itself
questions.why: RFC 8288 web linking lets a response advertise related URLs with relation types; GitHub sends `Link: <...page=3>; rel="next", <...>; rel="last"`. Cross-origin frontends also need `Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Link` to read it.

questions.q: An HTML form uploads a file with `enctype="multipart/form-data"`. What does the body look like?
choices: A JSON object with the file encoded as a base64 string field
Parts separated by a boundary, each with its own headers and content
URL-encoded `key=value` pairs, with the file bytes percent-encoded
The raw file bytes only, with other fields moved into the query string
questions.why: Multipart bodies use a boundary string declared in `Content-Type`; each part has `Content-Disposition` (field name, filename) and optionally its own `Content-Type`. Base64 in JSON works but inflates the payload by about a third.

questions.q: In the browser, you POST a `FormData` with a file using fetch. Why should you NOT set the `Content-Type` header yourself?
choices: The browser must add the boundary parameter, which a manual header lacks
Setting it triggers a CORS preflight that forms are otherwise exempt from
A manual header forces the browser to encode the file as base64 text
fetch throws a TypeError if any header is set on a FormData request
questions.why: When the body is `FormData`, fetch writes `multipart/form-data; boundary=----...` itself. Setting `multipart/form-data` by hand omits the boundary, so the server cannot split the parts and sees an empty body.
questions.asked: A classic 'upload works in Postman but not in the app' bug that interviewers use to spot hands-on experience.

questions.q: Which body format does a plain HTML `<form method="post">` without `enctype` send?
choices: `application/json`, built from the form's named inputs
`multipart/form-data`, even when there are no file inputs
`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, as `a=1&b=2` pairs
`text/plain`, with one field per line of the request body
questions.why: URL-encoded is the default; you opt into multipart for files. Express 5 needs `express.urlencoded()` to parse it and ASP.NET Core binds it with `[FromForm]`, whereas `express.json()` would ignore such a body.

questions.q: An Express 5 route reads `req.body.email` and it is always `undefined`, even though the client sends JSON. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Express 5 removed `req.body`, so it must now be read from `req.json()`
JSON bodies are only parsed on PUT, so a POST route never gets them
The client omits `Content-Type: application/json`, so the parser skips it
The route handler is not `async`, so the body has not arrived yet
questions.why: `express.json()` only parses bodies whose `Content-Type` matches, so a missing header leaves `req.body` undefined in Express 5 (it was `{}` in Express 4). Check the header in the network tab before blaming the server.
questions.asked: A debugging question: strong candidates check the request headers in DevTools first.

questions.q: What does `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8` add over `application/json`?
choices: Nothing meaningful: JSON is defined as UTF-8, so the parameter is ignored
It enables emoji in JSON, which otherwise are escaped by the server
It tells gzip to use a UTF-8 dictionary, improving compression
It is required for browsers to parse JSON with non-ASCII characters
questions.why: RFC 8259 requires JSON exchanged between systems to be UTF-8 and the `application/json` registration defines no charset parameter. It is harmless and common, but it matters for `text/*` types, not for JSON.

questions.q: What is `Expect: 100-continue` used for on a large upload?
choices: It asks the server to compress the upload as it arrives
It lets the server reject by headers before the body is sent
It tells the server to resume a partly finished upload
It tells proxies to keep the connection open for 100 seconds
questions.why: The client sends headers and waits for a `100 Continue` interim response; if auth or size checks fail the server replies 401 or 413 straight away and the gigabyte body is never transmitted. curl does this automatically for large bodies.

questions.q: What is `103 Early Hints` for?
choices: Warning the client that the final response will be an error
Sending `Link` preload headers while the server still builds the page
Telling the client to retry the request at a nearby edge server
Signalling that the response body will arrive in many small chunks
questions.why: 103 is an interim response carrying `Link: <...>; rel=preload` headers, so the browser starts fetching CSS and fonts while the origin is still rendering. CDNs often generate it from cached headers.

questions.q: What does HTTP keep-alive (persistent connections) save?
choices: The server's session state, which would otherwise be lost between calls
The TCP and TLS handshakes, by reusing one connection for many requests
Bandwidth, by keeping a compressed copy of each response in memory
Authentication, by remembering the first request's `Authorization` header
questions.why: Opening a TLS connection costs several round trips; reusing it avoids that. It has nothing to do with application sessions: each request is still independent and must carry its own credentials.
questions.asked: Leads into why creating a new `HttpClient` per request in .NET exhausts sockets.

questions.q: A .NET service creates `new HttpClient()` inside every request handler and disposes it. Under load it fails with socket errors. Why?
choices: HttpClient is not thread-safe, so concurrent handlers corrupt it
Disposed clients leave sockets in TIME_WAIT, exhausting local ports
Each HttpClient opens a new thread, exhausting the thread pool
HttpClient caches every response in memory until it is disposed
questions.why: Each disposal closes its connections, which linger in TIME_WAIT, so a burst uses up ephemeral ports. Use `IHttpClientFactory` (typed or named clients) or a long-lived client with `PooledConnectionLifetime` so DNS changes are still picked up.
questions.asked: One of the most famous .NET HTTP pitfalls; strong answers mention the DNS-staleness problem with a singleton too.

questions.q: Is `/api/Users` the same resource as `/api/users`?
choices: Yes, URLs are case-insensitive throughout, by the HTTP spec
Only the host is case-insensitive; the path may be case-sensitive
Yes, but only when the server runs on a Windows host machine
No, and the query string is also always compared case-sensitively
questions.why: Scheme and host are case-insensitive; path comparison is up to the server. ASP.NET Core routing is case-insensitive by default while Express is not unless configured, and caches treat the two as separate keys. Pick lowercase and stick to it.

questions.q: What should `GET /api/orders/abc` return when order ids are integers?
choices: 500, because the database throws when parsing `abc` as an integer
400 or 404, decided once and applied consistently across the API
200 with `null`, because no order with that id could be found
422, because the id is well-formed text but semantically wrong
questions.why: The request is the client's fault, so it must be a 4xx; ASP.NET Core route constraints like `{id:int}` produce 404, while explicit validation often gives 400. Leaking a 500 means an unhandled parse exception reached the user.
questions.asked: Asked to see whether invalid input can ever surface as a 500 in your API.

questions.q: A search endpoint's filter set is too large for a URL. What is a common pragmatic design?
choices: Send a GET with the filters in a JSON body, which every proxy forwards
Split the filters across several GETs and intersect results on the client
`POST /orders/search` with the filters in the body, accepting weaker caching
Store filters in a cookie so every GET to the endpoint carries them along
questions.why: POST-for-search is widely used when criteria are large or sensitive, at the cost of URL-based caching and bookmarking. Some APIs also save the search as a resource (`POST /searches` then `GET /searches/7/results`) to get a cacheable URL back.
questions.asked: A pragmatic design question; the strong answer names what you give up by using POST.

questions.q: Why should sensitive values such as an email address stay out of query strings where possible?
choices: Query strings are sent unencrypted even when the connection uses HTTPS
URLs are logged by servers and proxies, and kept in browser history
Query strings are limited to ASCII, so most email addresses are garbled
Browsers strip query strings from cross-origin requests by default
questions.why: TLS encrypts the full URL in transit, but URLs are written to access logs, analytics, history and sometimes `Referer` headers. Put personal data and tokens in the body or headers instead.
questions.asked: Catches the myth that HTTPS leaves query strings visible on the wire, and tests where data really leaks.

questions.q: What does `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (the browser default) send to other sites?
choices: The full URL including path and query, on every cross-origin request
Only the origin, and nothing at all when going from HTTPS to HTTP
Nothing, since cross-origin requests never carry a `Referer` header
The full URL, but only when the destination is also an HTTPS site
questions.why: Same-origin requests get the full URL; cross-origin requests get only `https://app.example/`; downgrades get nothing. That default limits leaks of paths like `/reset?token=...`, but tokens still should not live in URLs.

questions.q: Which headers does a cookie set with `Set-Cookie: sid=abc; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/` travel in afterwards?
choices: The `Cookie` request header, on HTTPS requests matching the domain and path
The `Authorization` header, because `HttpOnly` cookies act as bearer tokens
Every response's `Set-Cookie` header, so the client can refresh its copy
The `Cookie` header on all requests, over both HTTP and HTTPS connections
questions.why: The browser attaches matching cookies in `Cookie`; `Secure` limits it to HTTPS and `SameSite=Lax` withholds it from most cross-site subrequests. `HttpOnly` hides it from JavaScript but does not change how it is sent.

questions.q: Your API calls three downstream services per request, each with a 2-second timeout and one retry. What is the worst-case latency, and why does it matter?
choices: 2 seconds, because the retries run in parallel with the first attempts
About 12 seconds in sequence, far past a typical client or gateway timeout
6 seconds, because retries share the timeout of their first attempt
About 4 seconds, because only the slowest service's retry matters
questions.why: Three sequential calls times two attempts times two seconds is twelve seconds, so the gateway returns 504 while your server keeps working. Budget time end to end: an overall deadline, per-call timeouts below it, and parallel calls where independent.
questions.asked: Tests timeout budgeting, a real production concern that separates mid-level from junior answers.

questions.q: Which failures is it generally safe for an HTTP client to retry automatically?
choices: Any 4xx, because the client may have sent the request slightly too early
Connection errors, 429, 502, 503 and 504 on idempotent or keyed requests
Only 500, because it is the one code meaning 'try again in a moment'
Any failure at all, as long as the client retries it within one second
questions.why: Transient network and overload failures can succeed on retry, provided the operation is idempotent or protected by an idempotency key, with backoff and jitter. Most 4xx will fail identically; a blind 500 retry may repeat a half-done write.
questions.asked: A strong answer adds exponential backoff with jitter and honouring `Retry-After`.

questions.q: A client's retry loop gets a 429 with `Retry-After: 30`, but its own backoff schedule says to wait 2 seconds. What should it do?
choices: Wait 2 seconds, because the client's own schedule takes priority
Retry at once with a fresh idempotency key to reset the rate limit
Give up for good, because a 429 means the API key has been revoked
Wait at least 30 seconds, as the server has said when to come back
questions.why: `Retry-After` is the server's explicit instruction and should override a shorter local backoff; retrying early just earns another 429 and may extend a penalty window. A 429 is temporary, and idempotency keys have nothing to do with rate limits.
questions.asked: Good clients respect server hints; strong answers cap the wait and surface it to the user when it is long.

questions.q: What is a webhook's main advantage over the client polling `GET /orders?updatedSince=...` every minute?
choices: It is more secure, because the provider authenticates with a session
Events arrive within seconds and no requests are wasted when nothing changed
It guarantees each event is delivered exactly once and in the correct order
It needs no public endpoint, because the provider opens the connection
questions.why: Push beats poll on latency and wasted calls. But webhooks are at-least-once and may arrive out of order, and the receiver needs a public HTTPS endpoint, so a periodic reconciliation poll is still a common safety net.

questions.q: A webhook sender waits for your endpoint's response, and your handler takes 40 seconds to process each event. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing, because senders wait as long as it takes for a response
The sender times out, marks the delivery failed and retries it
The sender switches to polling your API for the event instead
The sender drops the event and never tries to deliver it again
questions.why: Providers typically time out after a few seconds and retry, so slow handlers produce duplicate deliveries and may get the endpoint disabled. Verify, store the event, return 2xx fast, then process it from a queue.
questions.asked: Shows whether you have run a webhook receiver in production, where slow handlers cause duplicate storms.

questions.q: What is the Richardson Maturity Model level 2, which most 'REST' APIs actually reach?
choices: One endpoint accepting RPC-style POSTs for every operation
Resources at their own URLs, used with the proper HTTP methods
Hypermedia links in every response guiding the client's next step
Separate URLs per resource, but every operation still sent via POST
questions.why: Level 0 is one endpoint, level 1 adds resources, level 2 adds proper verbs and status codes, level 3 adds hypermedia (HATEOAS). Most production JSON APIs are level 2, which is fine for practical purposes.

questions.q: In Express 5, what does this handler send?
choices: A 204 with the JSON body `{"ok":true}` attached to it
A 204 with no body, because Express strips it for that status
A 200 with the body, because `.json()` overrides the status
A 500, because Express throws when a 204 is given a body
questions.why: Node's HTTP layer and Express drop the body (and content headers) for 204 and 304, so the client never sees `{ ok: true }`. Use 200 when you want the health payload delivered.

questions.q: In an ASP.NET Core minimal API, which return declares both a 200 and a 404 in the OpenAPI metadata with compile-time checking?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/todos/{id}", async Task<Results<Ok<Todo>, NotFound>> (int id, AppDb db) =>
    await db.Todos.FindAsync(id) is { } t ? TypedResults.Ok(t) : TypedResults.NotFound());
choices: Returning `IResult`, since every `Results.*` call is described in OpenAPI
Returning `object`, which the framework inspects at runtime for status
Returning `Results<Ok<Todo>, NotFound>` with `TypedResults` factory calls
Returning `Task<Todo?>` and letting null automatically become a 404
questions.why: The `Results<T1, T2>` union plus `TypedResults` lets the compiler check each branch and lets the OpenAPI generator list both responses. Plain `IResult` works at runtime but hides the possible outcomes, and a null `Todo` becomes 200 with `null`, not 404.

questions.q: How many requests does a CORS-preflighted `PUT /api/items/1` cost the first time?
choices: One, since the browser attaches the preflight to the real request
Two: an OPTIONS preflight, then the PUT if the preflight allows it
Three: a HEAD, then an OPTIONS preflight, then the actual PUT
Two, but only when the request also includes cookies or credentials
questions.why: The browser sends a separate OPTIONS with `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `-Headers`, waits for approval, then sends the PUT. That extra round trip is why `Access-Control-Max-Age` and same-origin setups matter for latency.
questions.asked: Links CORS to latency, useful when a mobile user complains that every save feels slow.

questions.q: In `GET /api/users/42/orders?status=shipped`, which part is a path parameter and which a query parameter?
choices: `42` identifies a resource in the path; `status=shipped` filters in the query
`orders` is the query parameter and `42` is the request body's identifier
`status` is a path parameter because it comes after the resource name
They are all query parameters, since Express exposes them together in `req.query`
questions.why: Path segments identify which resource you mean; query parameters modify how you see a collection (filter, sort, page). Express puts them in `req.params` and `req.query` respectively; ASP.NET Core binds them from route and query.
questions.asked: A junior warm-up; the follow-up is usually 'where would you put pagination?'.

questions.q: Which mapping of CRUD operations to HTTP methods is conventional?
choices: Create = PUT, Read = GET, Update = POST, Delete = DELETE
Create = POST, Read = GET, Update = PUT or PATCH, Delete = DELETE
Create = POST, Read = POST, Update = POST, Delete = POST with a flag
Create = GET with params, Read = GET, Update = PATCH, Delete = PUT
questions.why: POST to the collection creates with a server-assigned id; GET reads; PUT replaces and PATCH partially updates; DELETE removes. PUT can also create when the client chooses the id, which is why the mapping is a convention rather than a law.
questions.asked: The first REST question in many junior screens; strong answers mention PUT-to-create with client ids.

questions.q: What do the five status code classes mean?
choices: 1xx success, 2xx redirect, 3xx client error, 4xx server error, 5xx informational
1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx client error, 4xx redirection, 5xx server error
1xx debug, 2xx success, 3xx cache hit, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
questions.why: Clients that do not recognise a specific code must treat it like the x00 of its class, which is why the first digit matters most. 4xx means fix the request; 5xx means the server failed and a retry may work.
questions.asked: Basic, but the 'unknown code falls back to its class' detail impresses.

questions.q: A `POST /api/users` sends an email that already exists and emails must be unique. Which status is most informative?
choices: 500, because the database raised a unique constraint violation
404, because no user with the new email could be created
409 Conflict, because the request clashes with existing state
401, because the email is already bound to another account
questions.why: Catch the unique-constraint violation and map it to 409 (or a 400/422 with a field error). Letting it bubble up as 500 hides a client mistake as a server fault. Consider whether the message leaks which emails are registered.
questions.asked: Tests whether you translate database exceptions into meaningful API responses.

questions.q: What is an HTTP API 'endpoint' in everyday usage?
choices: The server machine hosting the API, identified by its IP address
A method plus a URL path pattern that a handler responds to
The last middleware in the pipeline, which always sends a 404
The TCP port that the API listens on, such as 443 or 8080
questions.why: `GET /api/orders/{id}` and `DELETE /api/orders/{id}` are two endpoints on one resource. Thinking in method-plus-path is how routers in Express and ASP.NET Core match requests.
questions.asked: Warm-up vocabulary that frames the rest of the API conversation.

questions.q: What does 'stateless' NOT forbid in a REST API?
choices: Storing data in a database that later requests will read
Keeping per-client conversation state only in server memory
Requiring request 2 to go to the same server as request 1
Relying on the previous request's in-memory context
questions.why: Statelessness is about session context between requests, not about persistence: resource state lives in the database, and each request carries everything needed (such as a token) to be handled by any instance. Sticky in-memory sessions are what it rules out.
questions.asked: Catches the misunderstanding that 'stateless' means 'no database', which surprisingly many juniors hold.

questions.q: Why should a `GET /api/products` endpoint have a default page size even if clients never ask for one?
choices: Browsers cannot render more than a thousand JSON items in DevTools
HTTP limits JSON responses to 1 MB unless the body is chunked
CDNs refuse to cache responses that are over a certain size
An unbounded result grows with the table and eventually times out
questions.why: A collection that is small in development can hold millions of rows in production, turning one request into a slow query, huge payload and memory spike. Default and cap the page size server-side.
questions.asked: Tests production thinking; strong answers mention capping client-provided limits too.

questions.q: What is the difference between 401 and 407?
choices: 401 is for expired sessions; 407 is for never-logged-in users
401 is the origin asking for credentials; 407 is a proxy asking
401 is for API tokens; 407 is for username and password logins
407 is the HTTP/2 version of 401 used for bearer authentication
questions.why: 407 Proxy Authentication Required comes with `Proxy-Authenticate` and is answered with `Proxy-Authorization`; it usually appears on corporate networks. Your app should essentially never send it.
questions.asked: Useful when a build or package install fails behind a corporate proxy, and to spot who reads status names carefully.

questions.q: A client receives 431 Request Header Fields Too Large on every request after logging in. What is the likely cause?
choices: The request body exceeded the server's upload limit after login
The access token has expired and must be refreshed from the server
Cookies or a JWT have grown so big that headers exceed the server limit
The client sent too many requests and is being rate limited by headers
questions.why: Servers cap total header size (often 8–16 KB); bloated cookies or a token stuffed with claims push past it. Fix by trimming claims, using a session id, or clearing stale cookies, rather than just raising the limit.
questions.asked: A real-world auth bug; strong answers mention keeping roles and permissions out of the token.

questions.q: Your API responds 200 to `GET /reports/2026` in 12 seconds. Which alternative design helps the client most?
choices: Increase the server timeout so that the connection never drops
Return 202 with a job URL, then a download link when it completes
Return 206 with the first rows and the remainder in later requests
Return 503 until the report is cached, and let the client retry
questions.why: The async request-reply pattern frees the connection and survives proxies with 30–60 second timeouts. The job resource reports progress and finally links to the result. 206 is for byte ranges, and a 503 would misreport health.
questions.asked: Strong answers mention a background worker and what happens if the job fails.

questions.q: The job-status resource `GET /jobs/7` reports that the job has finished. What is a common way to direct the client to the result?
choices: Return 303 See Other with `Location` set to the created result resource
Return 201 Created from the status URL with the report body inline
Return 410 Gone, because the job itself no longer needs to exist
Return 304 Not Modified, since the job will not change any further
questions.why: A 303 (or a 200 whose body contains a result link) points the client at the new resource with a GET. 201 describes a request that created something, which the status poll did not; 304 is only a caching response.
questions.asked: Distinguishes people who have implemented the pattern from those who can only name it.

questions.q: What is JSON:API or HAL, in the context of REST APIs?
choices: Security standards for signing JSON response bodies
Conventions for structuring JSON bodies, links and relationships
Transport protocols that replace HTTP for faster JSON delivery
Compression formats designed specifically for JSON payloads
questions.why: Both are response-format specifications: HAL adds `_links` and `_embedded`; JSON:API prescribes `data`, `relationships`, `included` and query conventions for sparse fields and includes. Adopting one saves design debates but adds verbosity.
questions.asked: Checks awareness that others have already solved envelope design, even if your team rolls its own.

questions.q: How can a REST API let clients request fewer fields without switching to GraphQL?
choices: Sparse fieldsets, such as `GET /users/7?fields=id,name,avatarUrl`
HEAD requests, which return only the fields the client specifies
Setting `Accept: application/json; fields=id,name` on the request
Range requests, which slice the JSON by byte offset to cut its size
questions.why: A `fields` (or `select`) parameter trims the payload, and the server must allowlist which fields can be selected. HEAD returns no body at all, and byte ranges would cut JSON mid-token.
questions.asked: Over-fetching is the standard argument for GraphQL; strong candidates show REST can address it too.

questions.q: A REST API supports `GET /orders/7?include=customer,items`. What problem does `include` solve?
choices: It makes the order cacheable by marking related data as immutable
It avoids extra round trips by embedding related resources on request
It authorises access to related data the caller cannot otherwise see
It guarantees that related resources are locked for the transaction
questions.why: Compound documents cut the waterfall of fetching the order, then its customer, then its items. The server still enforces authorization on every included resource and should cap which relations can be included.
questions.asked: Leads into N+1 queries on the server, since each include needs an efficient join or batch load.

questions.q: In a .NET 9 minimal API, what does `app.MapGet("/items/{id:int}", ...)` do with `GET /items/abc`?
choices: Binds `id` as 0 and runs the handler, which then returns a 404
Returns 400 with a problem details body naming the `id` parameter
Returns 404, because the route constraint means no endpoint matches
Throws a `FormatException`, which becomes a 500 without a handler
questions.why: Route constraints participate in matching, so `abc` fails `int` and no endpoint is selected, giving 404. Constraints are for disambiguating routes; validation that should produce a 400 belongs in the handler or a filter.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand routing versus validation in ASP.NET Core.

questions.q: What is the role of the `User-Agent` header for an API?
choices: It authenticates the calling application, like an API key
It identifies the client software, useful for logs and support
It tells the server which response format the client wants
It is required to pass CORS checks on cross-origin requests
questions.why: It is a self-reported client identifier, trivially spoofed, so it is useful for diagnostics and analytics but never for security. Some APIs, such as GitHub's, require a descriptive one so they can contact misbehaving integrators.
questions.asked: Checks that you do not trust client-supplied identity headers for security decisions.

questions.q: A React app calls the API with `fetch('/api/orders', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(order) })` and the server sees an empty body. What is missing?
choices: The `mode: 'cors'` option, without which POST bodies are stripped
A `headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }` entry
`await` before `JSON.stringify`, as serialising is asynchronous
The `credentials: 'include'` option, needed to send any body
questions.why: With a string body, fetch defaults the content type to `text/plain;charset=UTF-8`, so JSON middleware ignores it. The fix is one header; for same-origin calls neither CORS mode nor credentials is involved.
questions.asked: Possibly the most common fullstack bug; the strong answer is 'check the Content-Type in the network tab'.

questions.q: What does `mode: 'no-cors'` on a fetch actually give you?
choices: An opaque response whose status and body JavaScript cannot read
A normal response, because the browser skips CORS checks for it
A response with all headers readable but the body hidden
A preflight-free request that returns the full body as text
questions.why: `no-cors` lets you fire a simple request cross-origin but returns an opaque response: status 0, no readable headers or body. It is for things like caching third-party assets in a service worker, never a way to 'fix' CORS.
questions.asked: Juniors often reach for it to silence the error; the interviewer wants you to explain why it cannot work.

questions.q: What is `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` for?
choices: It encrypts cookies with a key that rotates every year
It tells browsers to use only HTTPS for this host for a year
It forces the server to renew its TLS certificate every year
It blocks mixed content by rewriting `http:` links in the page
questions.why: HSTS makes the browser upgrade every future request to HTTPS before it leaves, closing the window where an attacker could intercept the first plain-HTTP redirect. It only takes effect after one visit over HTTPS, unless the domain is preloaded.
questions.asked: Often asked alongside 'is redirecting HTTP to HTTPS enough?', where the strong answer is no.

questions.q: What should the `Allow` header list in a 405 response for `/api/reports/9`?
choices: The roles allowed to call the resource, such as `admin, auditor`
The origins allowed to call it cross-origin, as a CORS header
The HTTP methods that the resource does support, such as `GET, HEAD`
The content types the resource accepts, such as `application/json`
questions.why: `Allow` advertises supported methods and is mandatory on 405. Roles have no standard header, allowed origins go in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, and acceptable request formats can go in `Accept-Post` or `Accept-Patch`.
questions.asked: Tests precise header knowledge; strong answers note frameworks add it for you.

questions.q: Why do Node and browsers not let application code set the `Content-Length` or `Host` header on fetch?
choices: They are forbidden headers the runtime controls, to keep the request valid
They are set by the server, not the client, so sending them does nothing
They are only defined for HTTP/1.1, and fetch always uses HTTP/2
They are deprecated in RFC 9110 and have been replaced by pseudo-headers
questions.why: The Fetch standard's forbidden request headers (including `Host`, `Content-Length`, `Cookie`, `Origin` in browsers) are computed by the user agent so scripts cannot forge them or desync the connection. HTTP/2 does use `:authority`, but the runtime still owns it.
questions.asked: Probes understanding of why browsers restrict what JavaScript can put on the wire.

questions.q: A mobile client lost connectivity mid-request, so it cannot tell if its `PUT /api/profile` was applied. Is retrying the PUT safe?
choices: No, because PUT is a write, and every write must never be retried
Only if the server returns a new ETag for every PUT it receives
No, because PUT always creates a new resource on the second call
Yes, because sending the same full replacement twice gives one end state
questions.why: PUT is idempotent: applying the same representation twice leaves the same result, so retrying after an unknown outcome is safe. The caveat is a concurrent edit in between, which `If-Match` guards against.
questions.asked: Applies the idempotency definition to a realistic failure, which is what interviewers want to see.

questions.q: Which statement about request body size limits in Express 5 is correct?
choices: Express has no limit, so a proxy must enforce one in front of it
`express.json()` defaults to a 100 KB limit and returns 413 above it
`express.json()` rejects bodies over 1 MB with a 400 Bad Request
Limits apply only to multipart uploads, not to JSON request bodies
questions.why: The body-parser behind `express.json()` defaults to `limit: '100kb'` and raises a 413 error when exceeded; raise it per route if you genuinely need larger bodies. ASP.NET Core's Kestrel default is about 30 MB.
questions.asked: Explains mysterious 413s after a feature starts sending bigger payloads.

questions.q: A frontend shows a spinner forever when the API is down, because the request never settles. Which fix is correct?
choices: Add a timeout signal and render an error state with a retry button
Wrap the call in `try/catch`, since that alone surfaces network hangs
Switch to `XMLHttpRequest`, which always fails fast when a server is down
Poll `/health` every second and hide the spinner once it responds
questions.why: A hung connection neither resolves nor rejects, so `try/catch` never fires; a deadline turns it into an error you can show. Loading, success and error must all be modelled states in the UI.
questions.asked: Links HTTP behaviour to UX, a common take-home review point.

questions.q: What does `Connection: close` in an HTTP/1.1 response mean?
choices: The server will close the TCP connection after this response
The client must close the browser tab that made the request
The session has ended and the user must log in again
The server is shutting down and will refuse new requests
questions.why: HTTP/1.1 connections persist by default; `Connection: close` signals this one will not be reused. Servers send it during graceful shutdown to drain clients. HTTP/2 forbids the header and uses GOAWAY frames instead.
questions.asked: Relevant to graceful shutdown and zero-downtime deploys.

questions.q: An API returns a list of 50 orders, and the UI then calls `GET /customers/:id` for each row. What is this pattern, and a REST-side fix?
choices: Pagination drift; fixed by switching from offset to cursor paging
A client-side N+1; fixed with an `include` or embedded customer summary
Cache stampede; fixed by adding `stale-while-revalidate` to orders
Over-fetching; fixed by adding sparse fieldsets to the orders call
questions.why: Fifty-one requests where one would do is N+1 over HTTP. Embed what the list screen needs (customer name), support `include=customer`, or offer a batch `GET /customers?ids=...`.
questions.asked: Shows you design API responses around the screens that consume them.

questions.q: In the browser, which of these requests are CORS checks applied to?
choices: Only `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` calls that JavaScript makes
Every cross-origin request, including `` and `
Cross-origin script-read requests, and `crossorigin`-marked tags
Only requests that carry cookies or an `Authorization` header
questions.why: CORS governs whether scripts may read cross-origin responses: fetch, XHR, fonts, and tags that opt in with the `crossorigin` attribute (so canvas can read an image, for example). Plain `` and `
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand CORS protects reading, not loading.
